slides.body: Your CTO has two questions. "The same commit runs on every laptop and fails in CI with a missing module. What is different?"
And the second. "One cleanup command deleted two days of labelled evaluation data. Can Git bring it back?"
The answer to the first: the laptops have a case-insensitive filesystem, one where upper and lower case count as the same name, and the CI runner, the machine that tests every change, does not.
Both failures happen at the border between Git and the filesystem.
Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
The first four are quick. The fifth, git clean, carries a red label, and before I run it I'll answer the five questions for a dangerous command out loud.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 4.12, one line at a time.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : A module was renamed from Config.py to config.py. It works on every Mac
                    and fails in CI on Linux, where the file is still called Config.py.
Git state         : The index and every commit say src/Config.py. The Mac's disk says config.py.
Mechanism         : With core.ignoreCase=true Git matches the directory entry "config.py" to
                    the tracked path "Config.py" and keeps the name it already had.
Root cause        : The rename was made in the filesystem only. On a case-insensitive
                    filesystem such a rename never reaches the index, so it is never committed.
Why Git does this : So that tools which change the case of a name on these filesystems do not
                    make a tracked file look deleted and a new one look untracked.
Correct fix       : git mv src/Config.py src/config.py, then commit.
Prevention        : Rename with git mv. Keep one naming convention. Let CI run on a
                    case-sensitive filesystem and fail on paths that differ only by case.

slides.direction: The mirror image: one tree with two entries, and the single file a Mac checkout produces.

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: A script fails in CI with "Permission denied". Root cause: it was committed with mode 100644; git ls-files --stage <path> shows it, and the fix is to set the bit in the index and commit.
An expected directory is missing after a clone. Root cause: Git does not track empty directories; commit a placeholder or, better, have the code create the directory it writes to.
A renamed file still has its old name on Linux. Root cause: a case-only rename made with mv on macOS never reached the index; rename with git mv.
Every line of a file shows as changed. Root cause: an editor rewrote the line endings; git ls-files --eol shows i/lf w/crlf.
git clean -fdx copied from an answer deletes the only copies of ignored data. Root cause: -x disregards ignore rules, and the files were never added, so no object holds them; run -n first.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. The typical loss, as the textbook describes it, is in an ML repository where data/, checkpoints/ and .env are ignored on purpose.
And the case trap is specific to teams that develop on macOS or Windows and deploy on Linux, which describes most backend and ML teams.

beats.text: File modes and symbolic links. In one sentence: besides its content, Git records one more thing about a file: its type, and whether it is executable.
beats.tele: File modes and symbolic links. In one sentence: besides its content, Git records one more thing about a file: its type, and whether it is executable.

beats.text: Precisely. An index entry and a tree entry carry a mode. The index is Git's list of what goes into the next commit, and a tree is its record of one directory. For files there are three modes. 100644, a regular file. 100755, an executable file. And 120000, a symbolic link, a small file that points at another path. The User's Manual puts it bluntly: "Git actually only pays attention to the executable bit." Owner, group, the other permission bits and timestamps are not recorded.
beats.tele: Precisely. An index entry and a tree entry carry a mode. The index is Git's list of what goes into the next commit, and a tree is its record of one directory. For files there are three modes. `100644`, a regular file. `100755`, an executable file. And `120000`, a symbolic link, a small file that points at another path. The User's Manual puts it bluntly: "Git actually only pays attention to the executable bit." Owner, group, the other permission bits and timestamps are not recorded.

beats.text: A mode change is a change: status reports it, and the diff shows old mode and new mode with no content lines. The mode isn't part of the blob, the object that holds the file's content. When the filesystem can't express the bit, you set it in the index directly, with git add --chmod=+x or git update-index --chmod=+x.
beats.tele: A mode change is a change: status reports it, and the diff shows `old mode` and `new mode` with no content lines. The mode isn't part of the blob, the object that holds the file's content. When the filesystem can't express the bit, you set it in the index directly, with `git add --chmod=+x` or `git update-index --chmod=+x`.

beats.text: Both are 🟢 SAFE: they change the mode in the index entry. With core.fileMode=false, Git stops comparing the bit. That's what git init and git clone configure when they detect a filesystem that doesn't keep it.
beats.tele: Both are 🟢 SAFE: they change the mode in the index entry. With `core.fileMode=false`, Git stops comparing the bit. That's what `git init` and `git clone` configure when they detect a filesystem that doesn't keep it.

beats.text: A symbolic link is stored as a blob whose content is the link text. Git never follows the link, and never stores the target's content under the link's path.
beats.tele: A symbolic link is stored as a blob whose content is the link text. Git never follows the link, and never stores the target's content under the link's path.

beats.text: Empty directories. In one sentence: Git tracks files. A directory exists in a commit only because a file path passes through it.
beats.tele: Empty directories. In one sentence: Git tracks files. A directory exists in a commit only because a file path passes through it.

beats.text: The index is a list of files, so there's nothing to add for an empty directory. The convention is to give the directory a file. A .gitignore inside it, with the pattern * and the exception !.gitignore, does two jobs at once: it keeps the directory in the repository and ignores its content. You'll also meet empty files named .gitkeep. The name means nothing to Git and appears nowhere in its documentation. The rule works in the other direction too: git rm on the last tracked file removes the directory.

The rule works in the other direction too: `git rm` on the last tracked file removes the directory.

When an editor on another platform rewrites every line ending, the whole file becomes one change.

beats.text: For the other four topics, one sentence covers them: Git's idea of a file is content, a path as bytes, and one of three modes. Everything else your filesystem knows is outside that idea: owners, other permission bits, empty directories, and whether upper and lower case are the same. Trouble starts where the filesystem's idea leaks in.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The typical loss, as the textbook describes it, is in an ML repository where data/, checkpoints/ and .env are ignored on purpose. Someone copies git clean -fdx from a "fix your broken build" answer, and the ignored files, which were the only copies, are deleted in under a second. The command did what its options say. The defence is the habit of running -n first, and of keeping irreplaceable data outside the working tree or in real storage.

beats.text: Let's land this. You should now be able to say, in your own words: Git records one permission bit, executable or not, and stores a symbolic link as a blob holding the link text. On a case-insensitive filesystem, a case-only rename made with mv never reaches the index, and two paths that differ only by case collide on checkout. I rename with git mv and detect collisions in CI. Git stores the bytes it is given, line endings included.
